transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Police in England say five people have been arrested near a U.K. air base that's used
by the U.S. military for strikes on Iran.
The men are being held on suspicion of a terrorist act that appears to involve three vans.
The base, Fairfort, has been used by American bombers for strictly limited strikes against
Iranian missile sites that deal was agreed to under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer,
who was opposed to the U.S. war on Iran.
Police haven't released details on those arrested, but President Trump praised the
arrests saying, "We had them under investigation," without giving more details.
In New York, at least one person is dead in the powerful nor'easter that hit the area.
Forecasters say the storm is slowly moving along the east coast, with heavy rain and
strong winds leading to flooding in New York City and New Jersey.
Governor Mikey Sherrill says shore communities have been hit hard and that they're monitoring
the damage closely.
Dozens of people have evacuated from their homes due to flooding, and dozens more were
rescued from cars and flooded roadways.
Forecasters say flash flooding is still possible in places.
The president's latest fight with the media continues after the White House blocked CNN,
which was TV pool coverage, from riding with him on Air Force One yesterday as Trump headed
to a college football game in Tennessee.
A federal judge ordered the White House to temporarily restore access last week, and
Piers Marlison has more.
Why is fighting the press good for him, especially if it ends up getting him less coverage?
Is that a good strategy for the midterms?
It's the same question that arises when you wonder why the president has taken so many
stands opposed to make majority public opinion on issue after issue.
On AI, the public wants regulation.
He says we shouldn't have any.
On data centers, the public's against them, he says the only people who are against data
centers are people who want to be, quote, "poor and backwards."
He's for flock cameras, the public doesn't like them, and of course, he's for tariffs
and the war in Iran, two very unpopular policies.
And Piers Marlison reporting.
Pope Leo told a massive crowd gathered at the Shrine of Lourdes that the Catholic Church
has to confront deep wounds caused by clergy abuse.
And Piers Eleanor Beardsley reports Leo is on a four-day visit to France.
Lourdes is a town in the foothills of the Pyrenees Mountains that attracts some three
million pilgrims a year for its purported healing spring waters on the spot where a
19th-century shepherd girl had apparitions of Virgin Mary.
The site is also connected to a recent scandal.
The Shrine's façade has a series of mosaics by a prominent religious artist accused of
abusing 20 women.
The story's tall mosaics have been covered for the pope's visit.
Leo has previously apologized for abuse scandals that have damaged the church's credibility.
On a trip to Spain in June, he told bishops they must listen to survivors and offer reparations.
Eleanor Beardsley reporting.
This is NPR News.
Russian attacks across Ukraine overnight killed at least three people after Moscow rejected
German calls to ease its escalation toward NATO.
Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, dismissed a meeting with his German counterpart
at the UN General Assembly in New York last week, saying it lacked "genuine dialogue."
Tensions between Russia and Germany have worsened after a drone attack at Leipzig Airport last
month.
Meanwhile, Moscow continues to target Ukraine with missiles and drones while Kiev strikes
Ukrainian Russian oil refineries.
Moscow's war shows no sign of slowing, and both sides are blaming each other for ongoing
hostilities.
Voters in Switzerland said a resounding no to proposals to make their traditional neutrality
more strict.
As Imogene Folks reports, the size of the defeat reflects a growing realization that
trying to ignore today's conflicts is neither morally nor strategically a good idea.
The result, 70 percent of those voting rejected the proposals, suggest most Swiss believe
neutrality cannot ignore international law or reward aggression, and that to protect
their own country, new alliances with European neighbors may be necessary.
They also doubted the motivations of a key supporter of strict neutrality, right-wing
political and business leader Christoph Blocher.
His companies traded with apartheid South Africa and were trading with Russia until
sanctions were imposed.
For NPR News, I'm Imogene Folks in Bairn.
And I'm Janine Herbst, and you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
